utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is the 1st of May. My greetings to all the people in the courtroom, the Prosecution Bench, and the Defence counsel, and the accused. As you know, we are going to have a witness over three days this week. The Trial Chamber therefore counted four hours for the Prosecution, same amount of time for the Defence counsel, among which one hour for Mr. Pusic. In other words, the remaining three hours will be spread among the other accused. So this is the way the proceedings are going to unfold. We're going to bring in the witness for him or her to make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I'm going to first check that you can hear me in your own language. If this is so, say you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have understood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution, and before I ask you to make your solemn declaration for the record, I'd like you to state your first name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Alija Lizde, the 1st of September, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a journalist, graduated from the faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For which newspaper do you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a private radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, you work in the media, in the radio. What is the name of your private radio station, in case the Judges want to listen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radio Stari Most, meaning Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Radio Stari Most. Sir, have you had an opportunity to testify before a national or international Tribunal as to the facts that happened in your country or is this the first time you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time that I'm testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a few words by way of explanation as to the way the hearing is going to take place. It is a hearing devoted to your testimony over several days. First you're going to be put questions by the Prosecution. You must have met some representatives of the OTP yesterday or this morning or over the weekend, I don't know exactly, and the OTP representative is going to ask questions of you, and you will have to answer them. Once this stage is over, it may take several hours, and there may also be documents that are going to be submitted to you by the Prosecutor. We have a series of documents, seven in all right now. They're supposed to be submitted to you to elicit some comments from you on them. So once this phase is over, the Defence counsel, who are on your left, or the accused themselves, may ask questions of you as part of what is called the cross-examination, and during cross-examination some documents may be presented to you. You have four Judges in front you. They, too, at any time can ask questions, but for a while now we have thought it better, for convenience purposes, not to ask questions right now. We prefer to ask questions once everybody's asked their own questions, unless it is absolutely necessary to intervene. Try to provide clear answers, because you know these are oral proceedings, and everything you say is going to be recorded on this transcript you have on the monitor in English, and it is scroll -- unscrolling as everybody is speaking. So do endeavour to provide clear answers. If you fail to understand a question, please do not hesitate. Ask the person asking the question to rephrase it. As a rule, we have a break every 90 minutes. We break for 20 minutes for technical reasons, and also to give everybody a rest. This being said, if at any time you feel the need to have a rest or if you don't feel well, there again do not hesitate to tell us so, because then I can stop the proceedings straight away, should this be necessary. So this is just in a few words the way the questions are going to be put to you, and this is the way the hearing is going to take place. You have sworn, made a solemn declaration to tell the truth, which means that you are not allowed to say -- to tell any lie. Now you are a witness of this Tribunal, and this must guide your answers. But you understand this because you are a journalist, and as such you're bound to have been interested in proceedings and this type of proceedings. I don't know who's going to be examining you. Yes, this is Mr. Poryvaev. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, I would just like to remind you that the other day we agreed upon that you will not speak too fast. As a professional journalist, of course you speak very fast, and don't please make a lot of trouble to our interpreters here in the courtroom. And then another issue that I would like to clarify. Again during our conversation you told me that you did testify once before a Sweden court. Could you just inform briefly the Trial Chamber in what kind of proceedings did you participate in Sweden?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I wasn't in Sweden, but I testified by videolink from Sarajevo. I forgot to say that. I was going to say that by the by, but what I thought I was being asked is whether I had ever testified before here in this court, in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you testify about the crimes committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Relevant to what area?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, the stories linked to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the moment. If it's necessary, we'll come back to this issue later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: With your leave, Your Honour, I'll try to pass through some background issues by leading our witness. There is nothing special in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, is it correct that before the Serb aggression started you were a journalist writing for the publishing house Vjesnik in Zagreb? Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When the fight against the Serbs started, you -- in April 1992, you joined the Mostar Battalion as a foot soldier. I mean the Mostar Battalion of ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: On the 30th of June -- 13th of June you were badly wounded - 13th of June, sorry, yes - on the front lines, and --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The 30th [as interpreted]. The 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. 1992, and were taken to hospital where you stayed until the 16th of August, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you go back to your military unit after you had left the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of job or service were you given there, if any?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, I began working in the information and propaganda field of the 1st Mostar Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What exactly was your position called?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: At the beginning I was just a member of the information and propaganda service of the 1st Mostar Brigade, and later on assistant to the commander of the IPS of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In some other documents your position is called as the head of information and perhaps. It would be also correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way. It's a question of interpretation, how you interpret, things. Head or assistant to the commander, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Did you remain in the same position when the 4th Corps was established in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I was appointed there in the 4th Corps to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I mean the head of information and propaganda. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. I was appointed as head in the 4th Corps. But in the 1st Mostar Brigade I was just a member of the management of the IPS, the Information and Propaganda Service. I wasn't the head in the 1st Mostar Brigade. I was the head in the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And who was your immediate commander? In the 4th Corps, I mean.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: General Arif Pasalic, the late General Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you continue any kind of job as a journalist for some military newspapers at that period of time when you were within the Mostar Brigade and then within the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for Mostarsko Jutro, which is the newspaper of the 1st Mostar Brigade. Later on I worked at radio Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Mostar studio and in the Hercegovacki Vojnik or Herzegovinian soldier which is a paper of the 4th Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, did you take any part in the establishment of the War Mostar Studio in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Not directly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But do you know why was that -- there was studio established?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The studio was established because in Mostar in 1992 there was one radio station which was called Radio Mostar, only one, and very shortly it changed its name into Croatian Radio Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But was it only the matter of name or the context of the programme also changed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, with the change of name, the context changed, too. The contents changed, too, very shortly afterwards. They only used one language which they called the Croatian Krugovalna Postaja Mostar. They changed the contents, I mean the information that they put out that you could hear, the music that they played. And with the establishment of the war studio of Bosnia-Herzegovina, something else was formed which could be termed multi-cultural for Mostar and for Bosnia-Herzegovina as an a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And could you tell us who was -- who were the people who actually set up the War Mostar Studio?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: As far as the establish. The War Studio Mostar itself is concerned, I think that in large measure this was a political decision to set up this war studio. When I say political decision, it was of the leaders of the SDA party principally amongst whom as the extended arm you had Dzemal Hamzic, the journalist, Asim Manjgo as well, and perhaps Omer Vatric, perhaps Sahovic, that team of people, professional journalist. And Asim Manjgo who worked in radio Mostar. When this chained its name to the Croatian radio he was let go. He was dismissed. And then he took part in the form's and establishment of this other radio station, and I was a member of the editorial board, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Very briefly. What was the purpose of setting up this alternative, the war studio?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, the purpose was that the citizens of Mostar could hear another truth, because in Mostar there were many people who had mixed marriages. The majority of the population were Bosniaks, and the idea was -- in its inception was to cater to this. And on the editorial board there were both Serbs and Croats, and we wanted to fight for Bosnia and its multi-culturalism, which is what the situation is like today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, did you retain your membership in the 4th Corps when you became member of the war studio?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And did you remain in the same position as the head of information and propaganda?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any military rank?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you wear military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: From time to time. Actually, mostly I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just very briefly, was -- what was your particular line of duties? In the radio station, I mean, in the war studio station.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: In the war studio I was the editor of the information and political programme. That means I dealt with the news, the news bulletin, the daily news bulletin, and I had a few other programmes where I would invite guests to speak. So these were daily duties within the frameworks of the information programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What sources of information did you have?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: In view of the situation in town and the media blockade, especially from that other part of Sarajevo, we had a lot of young associate journalists who went round town. It was a local radio station. You could just hear it in -- pick it up in Mostar. And Slobodna Dalmacija and some other newspapers and people who came from there, who came to Mostar from there. And you could watch Croatian television mostly. But you could say that the number of information that came in was selected by our young journalists who were in town every day collecting information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was it -- was it possible for your young journalists to go just outside of Mostar for collecting information?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't possible. Almost nobody could leave without having a lot of papers and permits. And this applied to journalists too. If anybody did go, then that would be people from the editorial offices. So that I, for example, once went to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stop a little bit. We'll go back to Prozor a little bit later. Did you have -- I mean, now talking about the war studio. Did you have any contacts with ABiH command?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, we did have contacts. First of all, we were physically close by, just some 10 metres away from the commander's office, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Where did you have your headquarters? I mean your particular place.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The radio was in the Vranica building, which is where the command of the 1st Mostar Brigade was of the 4th Corps. The 1st Mostar Brigade was in the cellar and on the first floor in a hallway, at the end of the hallway there was the radio and then in that part of the hallway as well you had the 4th Corps command HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you ever take interview from Mr. Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was your war studio recognised by the official HVO authorities?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No. We did not receive regular reports that our colleagues at the Croatian radio station got. Arif Pasalic was not able to be a guest on Croatian radio, for example, so we were sort of working underground, if I can it that way, or we were considered illegal as far as they were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You just told the Chamber that on some -- at some point you went to Prozor for collecting some information. First of all, when did it take place?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: In October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I think it was on the 21st, actually. And I went to Prozor after a press conference, which was held daily in the Projektant building on the premises there. When the porte-parole for the Croatian Defence counsel Mr. Bozic Rajic and Mr. Srecko Vucina tried to convince the journalists, and there was some -- there was some information to the effect that something had happened. There had been some sort of conflict and that there were problems in Prozor, but they said that nothing had happened in Prozor, and if any of the journalists wanted to go they could do so. I expressed the desire to go with a colleague of mine, a photographer and a driver, and we received a permit, a piece of paper to go, and I used the Vjesnik accreditation I had and we went it to Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you report to the HVO authorities in Prozor, I mean reported your arrival?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, we had -- there were a lot of -- there was a lot of control and checking before we actually entered Prozor. We were stopped by the police of the Croatian Defence Council. We arrived in Prozor, which looked terrible. So we went to the HVO headquarters which was the sole institution at the time. There were no other organs of power and authority. So as we passed through the town we could see houses were still on fire, and you could see traces of tanks having passed through the town, and what struck me first was that across the -- opposite the mosque there was a fire brigade station. That's what they told me. It was a nice glass building with large blue letters. It said, "Ustaski Dom." There were a lot of soldiers with red bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you manage to see the local Bosniaks on that day?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know who the Bosniaks were and who the Croats were; I couldn't differentiate. But there wasn't anyone there. The streets were empty except for the soldiers. There was absolutely nobody that you could see. It was only later when I contacted the commander, he didn't want to receive us, actually, he was in another building, I think in the Unis factory building or something like that, but he assigned a man to us who said that we could stay in Prozor for an hour, that he would take us around and he would tell it us who -- what we could film and who we could talk to. We were assigned this man, and that then we would be free to go. So we set off, and our escort took us to the -- took me to the fire brigade station, and I asked him whether we could go down there where the Ustashas are, and he said, "There are no Ustashas here." And I said, "Well, I saw the sign up saying 'Ustaski Dom,'" and he said, "Well, let's go down there." So we went down and the soldiers saw on my ID card that my name was Alija, but they said, "Well, you can go ahead and film. There are no more Turkish bullets in Prozor. You can see what the Ustashas are doing." And they said that the Bosniak civilians were all taken to a school in Rumboki, which is close to Prozor, another place close to Prozor, and we managed to make a few shots, take -- take some photographs. They allowed me to cross over to the mosque to ask -- to talk to the man there, but he didn't want to talk to me because he didn't know who I was and he didn't believe me when I told him. So the whole situation was quite terrible to behold.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, did you draft your, let's say, future broadcast about events in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, of course. My desire to go to Prozor in the first place was caused by my desire to put together a story, to get out the truth and to see what really happened. Unfortunately my report, my footage, was never aired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What happened? Why they didn't put your information on the air?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It was never aired for the simple reason that the next day at the time when our main -- the main news bulletin was supposed to be aired, the police chief of the Croatian Defence Council, Zeljko Dzidic, nicknamed Dzida, walked into our studio all dressed up and armed. He brought on him a piece of paper that he gave to me to read out loud on the air. That was at the beginning of the news bulletin. They knew that the news bulletin would be aired at 1600 hours that day. It was right in the middle of the radio programme when the news bulletin was about to be announced. I was given this slip of paper, and I'll tell you what it said: "By decision of the Croatian Defence Council, the programme of radio Bosnia and Herzegovina Mostar wartime studio is banned or abolished until further notice." There was nothing I could do. The announcer was there and the sound engineer was there. We were the only people. So I just read out this slip of paper and I told my listeners, "You'll probably hear from us soon again." I remember full well this was the last bit of news I read on that day, the very last sentence. I read the news about the curfew in Mostar, that from now on it would be at 1800 hours and no longer at 2000 hours as it used to be. We just switched off all of our equipment and that was the reason we didn't continue to air the report from Prozor that we had prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see by whom that paper produced you was signed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I can't remember. I do know about this sentence that said that this was something that was being done by a decision of the Croatian Defence Council. I have no idea who it was signed by. Dzidic is the person who brought this to us, and he was the military police chief. So it was pretty clear who could have possibly issued him that paper. We were scared as well, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry. Did the HVO authorities represented explain to you why your radio station was closed down?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: He provided no explanation whatsoever, but he did bring along this slip of paper and the alleged explanation was that the radio frequency being used by us, 101,7 megahertz, was interfering with some other military frequencies apparently being used at the time by the Croatian Defence Council. So they had this interference with their communications system as the stated explanation for interrupting our work. But I still have my own private radio station to this very day operating at the same frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Did you undertake, and you and your staff manage to open the war studio?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Not me personally. I -- I did speak to the commander, needless to say, but the decision to open the war studio was made at another level, at a political level or a military level. There was some negotiations afoot, so among later we resumed work as usual. Unfortunately, I had no bearing on that, nor did the commander for that matter, for the radio to resume normal work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When you resumed your -- the war radio station, did you use the same frequency?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, the same one. I still do, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, were you ever arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: On the 7th of May and on the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. What happened on the 7th of May? How were you arrested and by whom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: My flat was near the Vranica building, the distance being maybe between 500 and 1.000 metres between the two. So halfway between the two, near the largest building in Mostar, which we normally refer to as Mostarka, and this was about midday I was in uniform and I was just walking down the street. It was a perfect sunny day. A civilian vehicle pulled up, a jeep of some kind or something like that. The vehicle disgorged two armed men carrying rifles. They pushed me against the body of the car and bundled me into the car while pointing their rifles against my neck. They took me to the Dzemal Bijedic university hall, which is just outside the mechanical engineering -- faculty of mechanical engineering. They took all my documents off me, all the sets of keys I had and everything. They opened the door to an auxiliary room, and they pushed me down a flight of stairs. So I came tumbling down to the cellar down there when I saw a young man in civilian clothes I knew him name I recognised him. I asked him, "What's going on?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, were you alone at the mechanical faculty? I mean, arrested person.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No. I just saw a young man downstairs. Half an hour perhaps an hour later this room, this cellar where we were was filled with civilians. Another young man turned up, Himzo Dzonko, in uniform. Within an hour the room was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any high ranking official at the mechanical faculty whom you considered to be in charge of the building?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't really know, but Mr. Berislav Pusic came down to see us later on. He walked up to me and asked what I was doing there. So I said, "I should be asking you the same thing. What am I doing here?" And then he said the army had arrested some of their men. So they decided to gather a few of us to have us exchanged. He said, "It wasn't us who arrested you. It was the army. But you will eventually be exchanged." He said something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you meet him during the war? I mean already in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Maybe just before my arrest. I had met Mr. Pusic in Jablanica. I think it was the SpaBat that had organised a meeting for the commissions for exchange of prisoners, the Croatian Defence Council, and the Bosniak side for prisoners from Jablanica, Konjic from, that area. He was there on behalf of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, and I was there in my capacity as a journalist. The head of the Bosnian delegation was Mr. Asim Catic. So I did see him that one time in Jablanica. The meeting took place in a tent of some kind. The meeting yielded no result, however. An ambulance had arrived or something, but no agreement was reached, and that was the one time that I saw him. I may have talked to him on the occasion but I can't quite remember if I did or not. I did know Mr. Pusic from before the war. He owned a business near the Vjesnik building, so we sort of knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When were you allowed to leave the mechanical faculty?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It was sometime that afternoon, 5.00, half past 5.00. There's one thing I need to point out, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean on the same day, on the 7th of May, yes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same day. The same day. But let me just say this because this is something that I have to say. Not a single young man, not a single civilian that was brought to that cellar, not a single one was brought there untouched, without being hit and beaten. There were people bleeding. There were people who were bruised. It was between 5.00 and 5.30 that day that they gathered all of us. They had us lined up outside the building. There is some kind of a corridor leading out of the building. There were police all around, lads caring rifles, lads in uniform. However, an order had just arrived for us to go back, apparently because the army had failed to release those people that they had previously arrested. So they just sent us back down to the cellar where we stayed for perhaps another half hour. They eventually released, had us all lined us up again, and let us go. They let us go out into the street the distance being about 20 metres and we were free. The Vranica building is under a kilometre away from the faculty building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Berislav Pusic on that day? I mean, later on the following day?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did see him. On the next day outside a cafe. I asked him to give me back my document. He said he'd then arrange for that the next day. "No problem," he said. I saw him outside this cafe. He was there with some lads. I walked up to him. I said I wanted my documents and keys back, everything that I'd had on me and that had been taken off me. He promised to give it back to me, but so far I've received nothing from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. That's about your first arrest and you just told us that you were arrested also on the 9th of May. What happened to you on the 9th of May? Of course, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Of course. On the 9th of May, at about 3.00 a.m., about a dozen armed police officers came to my flat. They told me to get my stuff, the basic necessities they said, and come with them. My wife remained behind in the flat with our two children. My son was five at the time, and my daughter was three. There was no choice. I was off. I put on my civilian jacket and off I was with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: They took me to the police station. It was at the time, and it still is, it's right next to the Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean civilian police station, MUP station?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did they interrogate you there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: People in uniforms. It was in a room. It was as soon as I came there. I think one of them was called Juric, but I can't be certain. In a way they wanted me to agree to work on Croatian radio. I said I'd rather not because I didn't think I would live up to the expectations and the professional standards of that particular radio station. That was my answer. I'm not sure why they made the offer at the time in the way that they did, but I did sort of -- of put the pieces together later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were you in any way mistreated at the MUP station on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, between the 9th and the 13th of May I stayed inside that building. Half the time I was handcuffed to a chair. I was beaten. I was mistreated. I was spat at. I was abused verbally. The worst day was the day when one of their own officers was killed, a police chief of some sort. His name was Lugonja. There were other people up there in that corridor. I was in the office for a while, and then they took me out into the corridor, saying that we'd all be killed. It certainly looked that way at the time. It was utter chaos. There was a lot of shooting. There was a lot of noise. It was mayhem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any other people who were arrested on the 9th of May and taken to the MUP station?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know where or when they were arrested. I just realised there were a lot of people in that corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: For example?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, for example, Vlado Fink, Nino Sefic, Zijad Emerovic [as interpreted]. Later Selma Dizdar, Bojana Mujanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: We -- I noticed a mistake. Zijad Demirovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Zijad Demirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Bojana Mujanovic and who else that you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I remember those three girls who were brought in three days later on the 11th, I think. Bojana Mujanovic, Selma Dizdar, Mirna Picuga, they were all outside in the corridor, and Dzemal Amdic [phoen] came later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Dzemal --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Dzemal Hamzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Dzemal Hamzic was the same as the chief in your studio.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. Dzemal Hamzic was the director of our radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And just one last question relevant to this topic. And what happened to the war studio on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, it stopped operating on the 9th of May. A shell fell on that building and hit the radio receiver that we had, and that was the end of it. The radio, that was history.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But did you have any reserve station before May 1993? I mean reserve station of the war studio.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Not as far as I know. Or at least not that I knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And where were you taken to on the 13th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: On the 13th of May or, rather, that night they took us out of the MUP building, the police station, and placed us all in a police van, a paddy wagon. We stayed for a brief while near the MUP building. They put the 15 or 20 of us in to that van and drove us to Ljubuski. We didn't know where we were on our way to, but once we arrived I realised that we were now in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And to what place in Ljubuski were you brought?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The van pulled over. We could hear voices inside. We didn't see anything. You couldn't actually see inside the van, and we didn't see where we were, but as soon as the door opened we saw lads in black uniforms, and it said on these uniforms, "Ljubuski military police." They took us inside this building. The building is still a police station. We were in this corridor --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just to -- you said that they took us from MUP station to Ljubuski. Whom do you mean by who -- "they"? Who escorted you to Ljubuski from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Police. Police. The same people who had previously brought me to the police station. Police officers. I'm not sure how many vehicles there were ahead of us, but there was a police officer on the front seat in the driver's seat and we were on the back seat. It was the military police or just plain police. They had police uniforms on. I don't think you could possibly expect to find anybody else in the police station, could you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. So you were brought to Ljubuski, and in particular to the police station, military police station. And now I would like Witness to be shown Exhibit P 090 -- sorry, P 0 -- P 09089. Mr. Lizde, do you recognise this drawing?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That I produced this drawing myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who performed the text in English?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The people who interviewed me. Investigators, I suppose, interpreters, whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what is --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I drew this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what is depicted there on this drawing?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: This is the entrance to the military police building. This is the door that we were taken through. It was a two-storey building in Ljubuski. This door to the yard and all those of us who were brought there --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Don't hurry. Perhaps you should take a marker, and since there are no numbers on this drawing, I think that it would be nice to have some positions here identified and marked. It doesn't the matter. Maybe -- Witness, do you prefer to do it on -- e-court is better, yeah.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Just put number 1 and circle it.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: This is the entrance, and this is the -- where we were first brought when they -- when they took us inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And what -- what happened at the military police station? Did they register you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: They had us all lined up against that wall over there when we arrived. They were in black uniforms, and they separated off from our group, a man named Rudolf Jozelic, a Croat, in put him in the middle of that corridor. He was a pilot with the BH army. They took everything off us, those who had something on them. They took our watches off us, that sort of thing, all the rest. I later learned that the name of this man was Ante Prlic. He beat Rudi, and half an hour later he ordered them to take us to what he referred to as number 7. I didn't know what it was at the time, but I did learn about what they meant later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Could you find your cell here on this drawing, cell number 7?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Right there. Shall I place a number there?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, number 2.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And just to then finalise with this drawing, just a couple of more questions. The cell next to yours, that cell and over here I see "Sovici detainees" there, the text. What could you explain about this, let's say text "Sovici detainees," and cell number 8?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The next morning when they allowed us to use the toilet that was nearby, this toilet was meant to be used by -- by the many people who were there, they told us in the corridor that the people from Sovici were there and that there were about 300 or 400 of those. This is a village close to Jablanica, and nobody knew at one time where those people were. So they were there, and some people from Stolac were there in a different part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just put on -- number 3 on cell 8. No, cell 8.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I forgot. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: This is, for the record, the cell where people from Sovici were detained. And now once you showed us a cell on the right side, and the -- I see here, "5-6 from Stolac." What do you mean by this text?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Five to six, yes. Five to six. This is where we found detainees who had already been there for a month. The political prisoners from Stolac, the prisoners of the SDA, the Merhamet. There were some elderly people, two professors. They were detained. They were serving a sentence of sorts. I don't know what. They had been tried in Stolac for their political activity or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please put number 4 and encircle this, and circle the rest, number 2 and number 3.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the drawing or this page please put your initials and today's date, 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll give an IC number to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document will become IC 529.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, since we are already -- you have already heard a number of witnesses from Ljubuski, I will not go through some issues already known to you and to everybody. It's maybe enough to make some conclusions. I would like to ask witness about some events in which he was directly involved and about his experience in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, were you ever mistreated at the Ljubuski military remand or prison?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I was. I was mistreated on four occasions. I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember the approximate period of time, or it's impossible?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I was in Ljubuski between the 13th of May and the 30th of May, from the moment I arrived until the moment I was released. With three other colleagues of mine I was forbidden to leave the cell and go anywhere. And we suffered daily interrogation and beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who was -- who were persons who beat you up?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The first were Enes Stakic [as interpreted] and Momir -- Romeo Blazevic. They were the two who arrived in Ljubuski. They arrived one morning maybe two or three days after our own arrival in Ljubuski. I know that when they entered the prison's yard they asked from the guards to release those men from Mostar, as they put it. And then the police officers who were in the prison opened the door and brought us out into the yard where they were waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please, Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Ernest Takac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's page 26, line 4. And Romeo Blazevic. And were they dressed in military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, they wore military uniforms. Ernest as we were on our way out looked at all of us and then he addressed me by saying, "You, beard, are here as well," because I sported a beard and then they took me to one side. Romeo took a shovel and hit Rudi on the head so heavily that for the first time in my life I saw a man without a nose. He actually pushed his nose into his skull with that shovel. I was standing on the side and they were ill-treating the others. They were spitting on them. The policeman who had opened the door and took us into the courtyard was standing next to me and told me that he would kill me and torch me as soon as it got dark because I, according to him, was a sharpshooter. I was threatened anyway. Then Ernest came and interrupted all that with a few blows, and then he told me that there were no longer any Muslims in Vjesnik. He knew me from the press conferences, I suppose. He grabbed me by the neck and told me, "I'm Srecko Vucina. Now you can put questions to me." There was a lot of ill-treatment, and when they had enough, the same policemen took us back into our cell, number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. The next fact when they were beaten.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: As I've already said that Vlado Fink, Rudolf Jozelic, and Abdul Haris, and myself were banned from leaving the cell. Every day between 80 and 90 per cent of the prisoners were taken to the front lines for work. They were taken to Neum. As far as I could tell from their stories they were taken there to dig trenches, and they were also taken to Ljubuski to work in the private fields as slaves. When people came to visit those detainees, they would find the four of us. One day two lads arrived and they were looking for a pilot. One of them had black buttons on his shirt. They were in uniforms. Later on I learned that his family name was Hrkac and that his nickname was Zdrala, and the other lad's nickname was Splico. First they took Rudi out to that courtyard, and after a certain while they re-entered the cell. They stood at the doorway and they asked the journalist to come out. Dzemal Hamzic and I stood up, went to the courtyard down the narrow corridor. To the left Rudi was lying on the ground blood soaked. We didn't know whether he was alive. And when I turned around I saw Dzemal lying on the ground. The guy with the black button on the uniform had already hit him. The blonde guy started hitting me next. They called him Splico. I tried to stay on my feet, and I did not feel any pain at first. Then the lad with the black button on his shirt approached me and hit me so hard, but he also said, "Look at this guy. He's very strong. I can't knock him over." But the beating was finished off by Splico, who was probably in charge of me. And the other guy was sitting on a chair and enjoying the scene. I can give you the details if you wish me to do so, but in any case, it was a gruesome experience. The military police that were in the building did not dare enter the courtyard. I suppose that they must have been observing us from the windows. And the two lads were probably re-educating us or something. I don't know what the idea behind all the beating was. I heard later on that the brother of the guy with the black button had been killed about that time and that he was probably trying to alleviate his pain or something. I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you -- yes. And the last fact, the fourth?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I would rather tell you about the third event first. When they searched through our documents, they found some papers that I had written. One morning they order all of us to come out into the courtyard. It was rather early in the morning, and the prisoner psychology is rather strange. We all -- all the time believed that there would be an exchange, that we would be released. And that morning when we were all taken out, we also heard that we would all be exchanged. However, when we entered the courtyard, the -- the prison warden, Ante Prlic, and the number of military policemen were standing facing us. We were lined up, and he was holding some papers in his hands. He said, "Alija Lizde, step out from the line." I recognised all these papers. They were my notes that I was making all this time. One of the policemen by the name of Petkovic saw that I was a journalist affiliated with the Zagreb-based Vjesnik. He came into my cell two or three days into our stay there. Everybody had to stand up, and he told me, "This guy here, he is a real genuine Ustasha. He worked for the Ustasha papers." He asked me what I needed. I said I needed cigarettes and a pencil. Every day he would come, bringing me cigarettes. But I was under the impression that he did it secretly. Later on it turned out that he had problems because of me. He had ended up in prison himself, but I'll tell you about it later. That's how I was able to make notes, because he had brought me a pencil. Mr. Prlic gave me a piece of paper to read from, and I was confused that early in the morning. I didn't know what to read. And then he snatched the piece of paper from me and read out the following sentence: "Here I mostly speak to Vlado Fink. I was beaten, but they are not even aware that they were hitting themselves. The longer I am here the more proud am I of myself." And then a policeman took a pistol and hit me on the head and threatened me that I would never leave this place alive. And then he said to the other prisoners, "There you have him. Because of him you won't have --"

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, go. Finish this sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry. [Interpretation] He said to the prisoners from Sovici, "Because of him, you will not be given food." They were even prepared, I suppose they were, but then people from Mostar intervened -- actually, for two days I was punished. I had to pull weeds in the prison perimeter or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When talking about Blazevic, Hrkac, and Takac, I would like to just clarify one issue. Did they belong to the staff of the Ljubuski prison or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, they did not work in the Ljubuski prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So did you recount all the stories about Ljubuski, about your beating, you being beaten?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No. And there's another one, a fourth one. The fourth one was Petkovic's story that I have mentioned. The guy, I suppose, was under a lot of pressure, and one day we were lined up. We -- Rudi and I were taken out of the line. At the time the military police wore yellow bands on their arms, and as they were leaving for the front line they wore those bands on their sleeves. Petrovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Petkovic"] first beat Rudi, and then it was my turn to be beaten. He had learned who I was, what my profession was. And at the end of all that he told me, "You have greetings from Arif Pasalic." All the policemen were on the windows. And I suppose when he did that, he reduced his own - how shall I put it? - shame for having brought me cigarettes. He had to save his face in front of them. That's why he beat me really heavily on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please stop. There is a mistake in the text, in the transcript. Just page 30, line 19, "Petkovic first beat Rudi." It was not Petrovic but Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Petrovic. It was the policeman Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, please. In English we still have the mistake on screen. It's Petrovic and not Petkovic that we should read.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Petrovic. Yes, now on page 34 and line 4 we have a rectification. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were you interrogated while you were detained in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I was interrogated, quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When you -- you said that you stayed in Ljubuski as from 13th of May until the end of May. That is the 30th of May, yes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And to where were you taken later, afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: To Heliodrom, to the building of the central prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You arrived at the end of May. Was the central prison full or half full at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: When we were brought in front of the prison in the afternoon on the 30th of May they lined us up. They counted heads. The first floor of the prison was full. There were lots of heads behind of bars, and we were accommodated on the second floor. The cell where I was also full. Everything was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see representatives of the Red Cross at Heliodrom compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I did at the Heliodrom but not in Ljubuski. I was even registered at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit P 09090. Do you see? Do you have this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I see that it's an ICRC card. And did you keep this card until the end of your detention in several detention facilities of HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, because I had hid them in my shoes in Dretelj. I kept them until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Then I would like you to take a look at Exhibit P 08894. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: This is also certificates issued by ICRC. I see here the date when you were registered, 11th of June, 1993. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And also I see the date of your release, 19th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And the last question relevant to this topic. When you were taken from Heliodrom, you said that it was 30th of June. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, it was the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened on that day? Why were you taken from Heliodrom somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a long time ago, and I really don't know to this very day why we were taken from Heliodrom. But they did. At the same time, long columns of people were brought to Heliodrom. They had arrived on foot, in lorries and buses. A group of us was taken away to Dretelj. Why were we chosen amongst everybody else, I don't know, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How many people were taken from Heliodrom to, as you said, Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I believe that there were three busloads. First they took us to the main road in a minivan, and then in three buses we were taken to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Let's go back to Dretelj. You said a number of buses and other vehicles were coming up to Heliodrom with people, loaded on them, and was that action in any way coordinated by some person from HVO or from the Heliodrom remand?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know. I had an occasion to see a lot of these people who were brought in every possible way. The person who was standing in the centre on a somewhat elevated plateau was Goran Cipra. I believe that he was the main coordinator. At least he seemed that way. People were not registered. They arrived in long columns. I could see all that because we had been taken out from the prison and we were waiting to be loaded onto the minivans and to be taken away. And we could see all that. It was all coordinated. People were standing in columns, in lines to be registered. Later on I learned that on the 30th of June the Northern Camp had been liberated together with Bijelo Polje and that this was the final cleansing of all Bosniaks from the part of the town under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know Goran Cipra?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What position did he hold at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I know that before the war he was a policeman. He worked in the police. And when I was released from the camp, the person who received me at the school of mechanical engineering was Goran Cipra. When we were released, he was the one who received us, which means that he was also at the faculty, which was the seat of the military police. Today Goran Cipra is a staff member of the American consulate in Mostar, which is a very interesting fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we could make a break now before I go on to the next topic, which is very hard, actually, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 20 to 4.00. We'll have a 20-minute break. We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, who escorted you from Heliodrom to Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The military police did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And how were you treated on your way from Heliodrom to Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, we all had to keep our heads down in the buses and to look in front of us. There were two armed policemen in the buses and we were crammed into the back of the buses, and there were a few seats up in front that were free, but we weren't allowed to look out of the windows or anything like that. As we passed through Medjugorje, and I know that area well, I saw it from -- by glancing askance, but in any event we all had to keep our heads down and that's where there was an international organisation, UNPROFOR, whatever. But anyway it was very difficult. It was the 30th of June. It was very hot weather. So it was a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So you arrived at Dretelj compound. Who was in charge of the Dretelj, let's say, prison.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It said "military police Dretelj," just as it did in Ljubuski. That's what it said on the building at the entrance, the gate. The buses parked there, and we would get out one by one. There were three military policemen sitting on chairs, and we would go up one by one for them to frisk us. And there was a whole stash of IDs that we'd received at Heliodrom. And as I saw this from the bus, I thought that this ID would mean something, but it turned out that it meant absolutely nothing. I put it in my shoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean the ICRC ID?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, the ICRC ID. I managed to hide it in my shoe. But I didn't realise then that it wouldn't mean anything, and I might just as well have thrown it away just like ought others had to do. The policemen told them to throw them away, the policemen that examined --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So on the territory of the Dretelj compound there were several hangars. Were you placed in one of the hangars?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In the upper part in -- of those buildings, in a tin, in a metal hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were there in your hangar?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, as we were packed tight, maybe 100 -- 800 to 1.000. That would be my assessment. Perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I can't help asking the witness, just to recount very briefly about the conditions of detention in Dretelj, because it -- according to witness it was the best -- the worst period in his life. But very briefly, because we heard a lot of witnesses on that.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: If I tell you that the most terrible black hole of Herzegovina, the Bosnian Croats, then that is certainly Dretelj. And I was in Dretelj for 19 days, but it seems like 19.000 years. There were 800 of us or a thousand or however many there were in that tin hangar. They gave us meals once a day. We would eat once, have a meal once, and we'd have to do it in 15 minutes. They would line us up, 11 of us at a time. I didn't know why 11, why they chose 11, but it turned out that the 11th man would take some bread from the policeman who held it, and then we'd all kneel down and break the bread up in the aluminium bowls that we had. They'd pour some liquid from a big pail and then we'd crouch down and eat until the policeman said enough. Then we'd have to run back, leave the receptacles or bowls or whatever, and the portion of bread that I received I would very often put in my pocket and then you'd find some crumbs later on and then you'd eat those crumbs later on in the day. But the worst thing was that we were left without water for three days. It was normal not to receive food, but water, that was really difficult. It was so difficult -- anyway, 800 of us had to eat and finish our meal in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, you just told the Chamber that policemen -- policemen would bring food and so on. Who were in charge of the Dretelj compound inside of the barracks, hangars? Who were your guards?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The military police, that's who. They were the guards. They were military police guards. And the people who arrived, who came to Dretelj to mistreat us and who beat us for the most part weren't -- except for the warden whom we knew was surnamed Anicic; I don't know his first name to this day. But anyway, as to it an example to us and to his policemen and all those had came in, a young guy whose surname was Sejtanic, who tried to escape one day, he -- in front of all of us, in front of the hangar, he beat him up so badly by way of an example, so that none of us would take us into our heads to try and escape. The policemen gave us food. They guarded us. I mean the military policemen. But the people who came to beat us were soldiers, special units of one kind or another. And in the court where I testified by videolink from Sarajevo - I forgot to tell you this - when they fractured my colleague's arm. The young man was a Swede. He was convicted for that act. He was black, and he was the member of a special unit called Dragan Bozanic or whatever from Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And just could you tell -- yes. You have already told us the name of that person who was beaten up. Do you know about any other facts of detainees beaten in Dretelj? Beaten or in any other manner mistreated. I would add that just to my question.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, there were the worst things happening that could ever happen to a man. They would storm the place in the morning with poles, with bottles of alcohol. They would open the doors to the hangar, and on one occasion a group entered. They said they were from Bijelo Polje, and they said that all the people of Mostar, Mostar men, should stand up. And all the people who stood up were either slapped or beaten with a baton. And when they finished with the people from Mostar, then they said, "Now, all the people who aren't from Mostar should get up." And then on another day some policemen -- well, from the compound, people wearing uniforms, those policemen. They asked the colleagues to slap each other. Mirza Cemalovic, nicknamed Japrak, and Hamdija Jahic, they had to slap each other. And the rest of us to watch it going on, and they just laughed. And then in the camp there was a young boy who wore a fur coat in that extremely hot weather, and the guards caught -- referred to him as Trebinjac, the man from Trebinje. He would enter the hangar and ask whether anybody needed any cigarettes, because if they did he could get them for them. Some of the people would give him some money or whatever because people came in daily from Dubravska Visoravan, the Dubrava Plateau, from the Capljina, from Stolac. And then he come back. He would return without the cigarettes, of course, and then the people asked for the cigarettes and all those who asked where their cigarettes were, were taken out and beaten. And I'd like to quote an example of my friend from Stolac whose name was Zenda who barely survived all the beating because he had asked for a cigarette from Trebinjac. He would come with a big sandwich, and then he'd eat the sandwich in a corner of the hangar. Now, the interesting point is that one day when they didn't open the hangar, that was on the 13th of June -- no, the 13th of July. I'm sorry, I misspoke. The 13th of July. We had no food and no water. And one day after that, it might have been the 15th, they shot for hours around the hangar or at the hangar. But as the hangar was constructed in such a way that it had these large metal -- it was made of a large metal framework, steel framework, we were able to lie down and protect our heads, because the bullets couldn't pierce the thick metal. But they did pierce the tin, and then the shrapnel from the tin wounded the people. They were injured. As was Halil Setka who lives in America now. He was a journalist colleague of mine. He was injured in the head. So that's a just small portion of all the things that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Sorry. Was he attended by -- by a doctor?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Nobody helped him, just us, those of us who were inside the hangar. There was a young guy who was a doctor. His name was Esad Boskailo. He was a doctor by profession, and he did what he could through words or something like that. But otherwise, nobody came to help us in any way. If you mean the guards or the people who did the shooting in the first place. Had they wanted to help us, they wouldn't have shot at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, do you know about any detainees who were killed in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do. I lost a very good friend of mine in Dretelj. His name was Omer Kohnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Omer Kohnic was killed. He died in a solitary confinement cell because Dretelj had these solitary confinement cells. He succumbed to his wounds after being beaten. And he told me afterwards -- or, rather, Dr. Kovacevic told me afterwards, the doctor who was with him, that after the beatings he was beaten on the neck or his Adam's apple and when they threw him into the solitary confinement cell he never regained consciousness. And there were some religious officers in the hangar, an Efendi was there. His name was Kasim Mezit. They took him away. The policeman told me that. They took him away in a Renault 4 with four dead bodies to bury somewhere. And later on it turned out it that was a Partisan cemetery. It was the Partisan cemetery at Modric. So that's what I know about those five people who were killed in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, were you ever interrogated in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. That happened too. They interrogated me. I think -- well, they came to fetch me in the hangar with a vehicle, and from the hangar to that other building the -- where the entrance was and where it said military police, and it's at a distance of a hundred metres, I was met down there by two young guys in uniforms, and judging by their accent, their dialect -- well, we can tell where we're from judging by our accents. They were Dalmatians. They introduced them receives as being the policemen of SIS or whatever, and they interrogated me. At the beginning they were very -- well, they were good. They allowed me to light up and have a drink of water. And they had their holsters but no pistols in them. But as they weren't satisfied with the answers I gave, they turned the table on me and ordered me -- ordered that I be returned to the hangar. I asked the policeman to let me go to the toilet. He said no. So I went back to the hangar, because in the hangar we defecated in a corner just five metres away from where my head was and where my other colleagues were in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, just let's go back for a moment to this shooting incident. Was Setka, Halil the only one who had been injured in the shooting inches tent in the tin hangar, or were there any other detainees who were also wounded?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I've already said that one of them was Setka. There were 10 to 15 wounded and injured people, but I knew Setka well, and he was close to me, just two metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was the tin hangar the only one which was affected by the shooting? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. All I do know is that on a daily basis in Dretelj camp you could hear screams and noise. There was a young guy (redacted). I have to tell you that story. He was well-known as a homosexual, and the military policemen would often -- to get their kicks, they would make him do all sorts of things with this man Trebinjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This might be something that could be handled in private session given the gentleman's -- I mean -- given the content of what -- I just think out of respect for the individual. I'm not trying to stifle the testimony, but I just do think that it might be sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So you were kept in Dretelj for 17 days. When -- where -- when and where were you taken afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. After Dretelj we were taken once again to Mostar and Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who escorted you there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Military police again, with large civilian transport trucks probably used for transporting cattle, livestock. With tarpaulins; anyway, they were transport trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When you came back to Heliodrom, were there more detainees than on the 30th [Realtime transcript read in error "13th"] of June when you left Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I left Heliodrom on the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, I say 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. There should be made a correction. Paragraph 43, line 15. 30th of June, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They brought us to the gymnastics hall which was full of prisoners, and -- well, we were exhausted. And they left us there in the sports hall which was full already. Well, it was full of people that I did actually know. They were all people from Mostar, or mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever see in Heliodrom any detainees who were not from Herzegovina but from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I saw them. I saw people who were from Central Bosnia, too. And we would refer to them as Bosnians in our jargon, but that's how the guards referred to them too when they selected them first to do labour. They'd say, "Come on, Bosanci," Bosnians. They were taken out first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know how it come about that they were transferred to Heliodrom from Central Bosnia through the Serb enclave?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, we talked to the people, and they told us. As far as I was able to gather, when they were rounded up where they had been living, they separated the women and children from the men. The men were put into buses. And at the border, whether at Derventa -- I'm not familiar with the area, but anyway, the area controlled by the army of Republika Srpska, the military police would enter - of Republika Srpska - take away their pistols or weapons from the military police which escorted the prisoners, and once they passed the territory of Republika Srpska they would give their weapons back to them, and then they'd go via Ljubuski. And they were detained for several days at Vitina, and after that they arrived at Heliodrom. Now, what was even more interesting as far as these people were concerned, sometimes at Heliodrom you would see International Red Cross white jeeps turning up. Then they would very often take the people away and hide them so that the Red Cross couldn't register them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, were you ever taken to perform any sort of labour outside Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken outside Heliodrom for labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: On many occasions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember how it happened?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, they would line us up every day. All the detainees would be lined up in front of the building. Let me just mention that I was taken out of the hall when I was brought from Dretelj and transferred to the school which is right next door to the hall. Otherwise, it's the building of the secondary military academy that there was -- that was there before the war. And every morning everybody would have to go outside, line up, and then they would select people. Well, the trucks would arrive, and people would go out to do labour. As I, and I said this at the beginning, was seriously wounded on the 30th of June, 1992, I managed to -- to get from a doctor -- well, there was some dispensary or whatever where there was Dr. Hadzic and Dr. Stranjak in the school. He wrote out a piece of paper which -- which said that I wasn't able to do labour because I was seriously wounded. So he exempted me from labour. So when the military policemen told me to go out and do work, I showed him this certificate from the doctor, and he said that didn't mean anything. And he asked me where I was wounded, and I said in Podvelezje. And he said, "Which people did you belong to?" And I said the armija, the BH army. And he said, "Well, that's precisely the kind of man we need." And I was taken to Santiceva, which is where we were held for seven days. We carried bags, sandbags, or whatever, and organised the trenches. We would make them -- roll them cigarettes, particularly grass, weed, and clean their rifles. And when I asked one of the policemen, the soldiers, when they would return us to the Heliodrom, because usually one group would bring us there and we'd stay there with those soldiers, those soldiers on duty there up at the front line, and then they would come and take us back and another group would be taken out. And this soldier sold me, "We can't take you back because the person that issued us -- issued you out has to see that you're returned." Well, I didn't really know what that meant. Usually people would stay for a day or two and then they would be taken back, whereas we stayed for seven days because the man who let us go in the first place wasn't there to take us back. At least that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was there any shooting when you were working on the Santiceva Street?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, of course there was shooting. As soon as we arrived they had us lined up outside the main post office. Several lads, soldiers. A German lad. He didn't speak very fluently, and we had trouble understanding what he was saying. There were several people who were wounded. The sharpshooter from the Croatian Defence Council and other people. That was a front line. It was only natural. The distance between an HVO trench and the army trench was no more than two metres. In purely military terms, that was quite common.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would like witness to be shown P 09398.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would only like at that say that there is probably a mistake in translation. In line 21 that -- that the army trench was no more than the distance between army trenches was no more than two metres. I believe that it should be probably 20 or whatever and not two metres. That is the distance between two trenches. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, could we ask the question from the witness, because I didn't -- that's the first thing that I noticed, that the gentleman said two metres, and so he must have been between the two metres.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
