utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to be more accurate about this, it -- it was about as far away as the street in a normal city, for example, about two and a half or four metres, and that was all the distance separating the HVO and the BH army. So how many metres can that possibly be? Well, it sure isn't 20, is it. For example, there was this area on Santica [as interpreted] Street. That's where I carried some sacks, bags, and the so-called drivers. On the one side of that street you had the BH army, and on the other side you had the HVO, and there was just a street between the two warring parties, and that street was controlled from a building, from a nearby building, a bank, a building that wasn't finished. As I said, it was a very small distance. I don't think if you looked anywhere along Santica Street you would have found a distance as large as 20 metres separating the two sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you just gave us a detail that just caught my attention. You said that there were snipers in the bank building, but whose sides were they on? Were they ABiH snipers or HVO snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These snipers, you saw them with your own eyes or was this hearsay? Were these hearsay that you heard, or did you actually see them, or did you actually hear the shots? Did you see the tracing bullets? How can you be so sure about their presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see the snipers. I didn't hear the shots for as long as I was on Santica Street, but my mates who were there before told me that a lot of the prisoners had been wounded there. I'm quoting exactly some of my mates from the prison. There were some of those who had spent each and every day on Santica Street. And I was asking myself the same question. How come it was impossible? Why couldn't they just run across the street to freedom? That's how I was imagining this. I said -- that was during forced labour. I could run for it, and they said, "Not a chance in hell." So many people came to grief on Santica Street. They were shooting at them. It's short street or, rather, a narrow street separating the drivers, because there was a motorist club there. Used to be before the war, and there a restaurant building that is across the street. And then there's that bank building which has now been finished. So I heard the story from people who spent every single day on Santic [as interpreted] Street and people who were wounded on Santic Street. They were shot by sniper bullets in the back as they were trying to cross the street from the stop of that bank building or office. Nobody got away. Freedom was so close but nobody got away. It was a stone's throw away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You gave us another detail. I thought I understood that you worked in the street.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's a street there, a street. A street. The street was the borderline. That's where I was carrying the sacks. I was carrying the sacks across to this restaurant that was across the street. Sandbags, sacks filled with sand. And the street is right underneath the window. I would place the sacks on the window, and then across the way there was the BH army. We had those sandbags that we were carrying. We constructed barriers because they would fire projectiles from the other side. It was a -- a very busy area. There were trenches being dug, and some of my mates went to Santica Street. They dug tunnels beneath that very street. There was a sort of tunnel being dug, so the street was all dug up. I never went into any of those tunnels myself, and I was not among those doing the actual digging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who dug the trenches under the street? Was it HVO or ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in that street. It was further down beneath. HVO prisoners were doing the digging. I was a prisoner who was preparing the sandbags for the soldiers on the front line. For example, if the BH army fire a missile blowing their barrier, their protection to bits, then we, the prisoners, would bring new sandbags in order to build a new barrier. Over the seven days I spent there on Santica Street I did precisely that throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... on the other side of the ABiH side, it was -- the same was being done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I was just a prisoner, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, I would like to just clear up the name of the street. Is it Santica Street or Santiceva Street?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Santiceva Street. That was what we called it. It's the longest street in Mostar. That's where the prison used to be, and there still is a prison on that street. So that's probably the street you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Now I would like Witness to be shown Exhibit P 09398. Witness, did you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a certificate [no interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is it a certificate you told us given you by the doctor?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My microphone still doesn't work. Perhaps if you turn yours off, Mr. Poryvaev. Yes. Thank you. Witness, you have told us that several times you were searched. You were asked to give everything you had to military policemen if I remember correctly. On the other hand, it seems that you have been able to preserve this paper. Was it that you were allowed to keep it or did you hide it as you hid the ID?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got the certificate at Heliodrom, which is where I was released from, but the certificate came towards the end of my time in the camp. The only thing that I managed to hide was the ICRC card. But they never searched me again afterwards, because I'd been in the camp for quite a long time by then, and they never searched me on my way out. There would have been nothing for them to find anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The certificate bears the date of 12 June '02. Were you at the Heliodrom at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12th of June, 2002. No. That's when I talked to the investigators, and I gave them the certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You did not have the microphone, or it didn't work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just take a look the figures. 12th of June, 2002, the date when the witness handed over the document to the investigator. It's not 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. You're right absolutely. I apologise. So this cannot be a certificate that he has --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- at the time he was working or asked to work at Santiceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would just ask you a question to clarify the situation. Did you get this certificate during your first detention at Heliodrom or the second?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No. No. The second time around. The second one, when I came from Dretelj. It was the second time around, not the first time around. I wasn't taken anywhere else. From Heliodrom to perform labour when I arrived from Ljubuski to the central prison. When I came from Dretelj, I went to that school building, the gym hall, and then the school, and that's where I got the certificate because the doctors were over at the school building. I got the certificate as soon as I arrived at Heliodrom the second time around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: My microphone is still on, so I take advantage of it. This is very strange, really, because it says clearly 12 June '02. That would be out altogether. The witness has been -- has left the Heliodrom for the first time on 30 June 1993, but how -- now, Mr. Lizde, you have said that you have received this when you got back to the Heliodrom. So it is a date later than 12th of June and certainly earlier than 2002. I cannot bring this all together. Is this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I first saw this date when I gave the certificate to the investigators who interviewed me, and they were the ones that added this in hand. This was not on the original certificate that I gave them. They wrote this themselves when I handed a copy of the certificate to them the first time I was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe the Defence will probe further into this. I leave it at that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, did you see any military units deployed at Heliodrom compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Of course I did. I did. There was this one day I made beds for -- for an elite unit that had arrived from Zagreb, the Tigers. The Split and the Vinkovci brigades were also at Heliodrom. And the one from Osijek. It was all right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did they arrive at the time you were detained at Heliodrom in June or in July or later?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know. The second time around when I was there I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see any artillery pieces on the territory of Heliodrom compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of artillery was positioned there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It was just next to the window in the central prison, just outside the window. We were locked up inside. There were some artillery weapons that being used to fire quite often, 120-millimetre weapons. That's what they told me. I didn't know about that at the time. And the 60-millimetre mortars. Those were positioned all around us, around the central prison building and the Kopex [phoen] building between the school and the central prison, in that area. I often saw the weapons actually fired for using. They were just outside our windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But do you know what positions were targeted by these artillery pieces from Heliodrom compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, the BH army positions. That's what positions were targeted, positions held by the BH army. I assume they were targeting them because there was no one else for them to target, was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, do you know of any facts of mistreating detainees at the Heliodrom prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Might -- might I just be allowed a question on the artillery?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, were the artillery pieces such as are drawn -- drawn by a lorry or other car, or were they mounted on a vehicle which is blinded and on caterpillars, which certain howitzers are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither. This was just outside our window. Some of it was actually embedded into the ground. Those were stationary weapons with wide barrels and with long barrels. I'm not sure how they put them there. I didn't see that myself. But I know that the weapons made a thunderous sound when used for firing, and this was the case frequently, especially outside the windows of the central prison building, which is where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lizde, I asked you about any facts of beating detainees known to you.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: At Heliodrom all over again, yes. There was this one day when nobody touched me, the second time around when I ended up at Heliodrom. No one touched me. I think a man named Mihalj, surname Mihalj, entered the school building. We were in this school, and each school has classrooms. There was a corridor. We were all shown to our respective rooms, and we slept on the floor. We all laid down on the floor. He came into our classroom. He mistreated people, beat people, and put out cigarette butts on people's backs, asking them to -- forcing them to do push-ups.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, did you see any high-ranking HVO commanders at the Heliodrom compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The only commander I knew was Mr. Petkovic. The reason being we had once travelled together in an APC. We drove from Makljen from Prozor to Vakuf. We were together in an APC, Mr. Petkovic, Mr. Arif Pasalic, and I. I knew him too. But not the rest. I didn't know Mr. Praljak, although I'd been told that Mr. Praljak was part of the delegation that arrived. I didn't know him. And even if I'd seen him, I would not have identified him. I did see Mr. Petkovic, and I did recognise him. The only dilemma that I still have is I can't remember whether that was during my first time there or my second time there. There were all sorts of delegations arriving comprising commanders of all kinds but, you know, there was a lot of fear --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Although the witness said he can remember whether this was in June or in July, given the time frame I would ask my learned colleague to ask another question about the exact time line to see whether the witness can be more specific about the time when somebody apparently told him that they had seen Praljak there. Otherwise, we will have to raise this in cross-examination and raise some sort of an alibi, but we can't spend the whole summer do -- doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic asked a question, but our witness has already answered this question, because he said he actually could not specify the time when he saw Mr. Praljak and Mr. Petkovic at the Heliodrom compound, whether it was during his first detention at the Heliodrom compound or the second which started in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, did you -- did you see them -- on how many occasions did you see them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't think that's the problem. He did not say he saw Mr. Praljak. He only saw Mr. Petkovic. But the others told him that Mr. Praljak had already come, unless I did not really understand the answer of the witness. So could you please repeat the question, Mr. Poryvaev, and reformulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Praljak at the Heliodrom compound?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I heard that it was Mr. Praljak. I didn't know him, and I can't say with certainty that this was Mr. Praljak. That's what they told me. They said, "This is Praljak. How come you don't know him? He's from Mostar too," that sort of thing. But I can't say with certainty. This is all I can tell you. Even as far as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, saw you a person, and one of your colleagues said that this is Praljak. This is the man from Mostar. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. And Praljak was at Heliodrom later. "You don't know him?" I said, "No, I don't." And he said, "How come? He's also from Mostar," and the second and third time round. The only way I know Mr. Praljak is from the media, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take it from the gentleman's answer he did not know Mr. Praljak at the time, did not recognise him by face or by media contact. So if the answer to that is yes, then it would appear that the gentleman cannot assist in this matter and it's mere speculation and we should just move on to save time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree with Mr. Karnavas, because the witness explained that he didn't knew Mr. Praljak, but his inmate explained to him that the person in front of them, just Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understood what the gentleman said. I'm just merely saying that this sort of information is meaningless and useless, and we should just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please. We know that this has been -- it was a long time. You were in Heliodrom a long time ago. But according to what you said, there was this person, and one of your co-detainees said, "This is Mr. Praljak." So the person you saw at the time, is it the one that we see here in this courtroom? Probably a bit older, of course, like all of us, but do you recognise him? Do you not recognise him? And he's even standing up, you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know now what Mr. Praljak looks like, but back then there was this group of people that passed me, and I couldn't possibly have recognised him even if I'd known him. So this man just told me it was Praljak. "Don't you know him?" I said, "No, I don't." Now I do know what he looks like. It's difficult to say, really. I heard that it was Mr. Praljak, but I didn't really have a chance to -- to look properly because they were on their way in. I'm afraid I don't have a good answer to that. Now I do know what he looks like, and I have known for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you seem to have told us that you have seen him three times. The second and third time, did you then recognise him because you had been told the first time who it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He's never recognised him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't say three times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] At least in Croatian the witness has never said that he heard about Praljak being there on three occasions. He mentioned just one time, and I've not been able to find it anywhere in the transcript either. And I can see the witness confirming this by nodding his head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness, you saw this group of people, and there was someone there from whom you were told that it was Mr. Praljak, and this person belonging to that group, you've only see him once, the one of whom you were told that it was Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just once and never again. Nobody ever told me again that he was there. I did not see him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's what I understood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have fell -- I fell victim to an error. I apologise. Thanks for clarifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. We would like to be able to save time on the cross. If the witness may be asked another question in order to be able to at least vaguely determine the time. Maybe he could tell us whether it was two days after his arrival, 20 days after the arrival, towards the end of his stay, at the it beginning of his stay, if he has any idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, this is not very specific, of course, but as far as you can remember, when your co-detainee told you this is Mr. Praljak, the man from Mostar, when did that take place? Was it in June, in July, at the end of June, at the beginning of July, or can't you tell us anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really can't tell you whether it was before or after. There is no detail in -- to jog my memory. I'm afraid whatever I told you would be wrong. I can't pinpoint the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the group of people we are talking about, are we talking about people who are dressed in civilian clothes or uniforms or both? Did these people look like officials, high-ranking officers as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the troops passed there is a lot of security. There are commanders. I was with the commander of the 4th Corps, and there were always four or five men with him. Whenever such a group passes there is a lot of guards with them, and I remember that there was a lot of guards, a lot of security. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're saying that there were people in charge of security there. Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course I saw that group of people that went by. They were passing by, and I saw them. Nobody stopped for us to see them. Whenever they arrived they would just pass through quickly. The only person from the command circles that was able to talk to us and ask for some people to cross over to his side was Juka Prazina and also Tuta, for example. We saw the two of them, but we never saw the others. They never spent any time. And the only thing you could see was through a little opening among the bars on your cells. That's why I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One point of clarification, Witness. Why did your co-detainee talk to you about Mr. Praljak, or did he point to all of these persons of authority who were there, or did he just point to Mr. Praljak? Why him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, on how many occasions did you see Mr. Petkovic at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Also when delegations came, but I'm sure that I saw Petkovic once. He was there once in the same group where Praljak apparently was. I don't want to speculate, but there were delegations, different delegations passing through in different ways, in vehicles, on foot. I'm afraid to make a mistake or to give you a wrong figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see Mr. Petkovic inside of the building, inside of the Heliodrom building?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the leading nature. He can ask, "Where did you see him? What was he doing?" Who, what, where, why, how, and explain or describe. Those are the questions at this point. So I would appreciate if the Prosecutor would just ask direct questions as opposed to leading the witness, even slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to join the objection by my colleague, Karnavas, and I would like to add that the witness has already answered the question because he spoke about having allegedly seen Generals Praljak and Petkovic through the bars of the little cell where he was accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Poryvaev. What do you want to stress here? The witness told us that there was this group that came once and where he recognised Mr. Petkovic. He knew him because he travelled with him at least once, and then he was told that Mr. Praljak was there, was a member of that group. What do you want to show here? What else do you want to point to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: The only thing that I would ask the witness just did he see members of the delegations, high-ranking delegations inside the building of the Heliodrom. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before he answers that question, the gentleman would first have to -- he has to lay a foundation. He's talking about high-ranking delegations. What are high-ranking delegations? In what aspect? Who did he see? He can ask that question. Who did you see that you would consider high ranking delegations? Name them. At what time, what place, what date, where were they, what were they saying, what were they doing? That's the direct examination of this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: We are talking about one delegation, high ranking delegation that the witness saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He has to lay a foundation, sir. He has to lay a foundation other than saying I saw a bunch of people with a bunch of other people surrounded, and therefore they are what constitute a high ranking delegation. I just think that this kind of testimony is irrelevant and is terribly unhelpful to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, the witness is telling us that this group apparently was standing outside. That's what I understood. I understood that they did not walk into the building. And now you're asking the witness whether the group went inside the building or the compound. When asking this question, are you thinking about other people than this particular group? Please try to be very specific because the witness's answer was very specific. He said that he saw people go by, but he did not say that these people entered the prison. But you seem to be saying that this group entered the premises. So please try and be extremely specific and to lay the foundations of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My question was quite simple. Did he see any people, high-ranking officials from HVO inside the Heliodrom building inspecting the cells. That was my question. That's not about -- specifically about Mr. Petkovic. There is some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, with all due respect to my learned friend, this is not a precise question. My learned friend is talking about a building at the Heliodrom. We have seen a sketch of the Heliodrom here, and we have seen that this is a huge complex with a lot of building. He should at least be precise and pinpoint the building. And this is exactly what my colleague, Karnavas, is saying; he has to lay a foundation otherwise we're going to waste time on speculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Poryvaev, we know because we've seen other evidence that the Heliodrom is a very large complex with several buildings. So when you ask him whether he saw high-ranking or prominent people, are you talking about the Heliodrom or are you talking about the prison's premises? You have to be extremely specific then because otherwise we'll have objections from the Defence and we'll be wasting time. So please ask a very specific question on that point to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Very specific question. Did you see any, let's say, commission consisted of high-ranking representatives of HVO in the building, in the premises where you were kept? That's what the question was.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's -- I don't understand why -- there is too much ado about nothing. Very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the whole points is that he has proofed the witness. He should have known that answer before he asked the question, and so why bother to ask the question if he already knows the answer? The answer is that there was nobody in that building and therefore it is a waste of time. It's not as if he's speaking with the gentleman for the first time. He's prepped him. He's proofed him. And all we're saying is to lay a foundation and move on as quickly as possible, because we're wasting time. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it's -- you are wasting time, not myself. My question was quite plain. I don't understand why it raises so many objections. It's quite a simple question, not only one to Mr. Petkovic. We clarify the situation with Mr. Petkovic and that was my final question about Heliodrom. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He answered that he saw no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear from him and for the conclusions that we would draw from this response, so it depends on what you want to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My next question is relevant to the time when you were released from Heliodrom. From the document, ICRC, we've seen that you were released on the 19th of October, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you remember more details about the day when you were released? When first you learn about the fact that you would be released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The day when I was released. A military policeman came, took me to the central prison from the school where I'd been. I had to sign a piece of paper. I did. The military police took us to the school of mechanical engineering in Mostar where the aforementioned Mr. Goran Cipra was waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you mean the same Goran Cipra you were talking about the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, the same Goran Cipra.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who else was present there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: When we were released?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Along with Mr. Goran Cipra.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: You mean the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: There were some people. There was a secretary. It was at the school of mechanical engineering, upstairs. Those were nicely appointed offices. Goran was on his own in his office, and he made a selection. He selected Selma, Bojana, and Dzemal. They entered his office. He poured them a drink and I and my colleague Sejo Beslagic waited in the corridor. When they had had the drink, he told us that on the following day we were to report to the office for exchanges run by Mr. Berislav Pusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just one question. You just told us that you had signed some paper. Do you remember what kind of paper was signed by you? To what effect was the contents of that paper?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I can't remember the content of the document. I only know that I policemen angry, those who had gathered us in the corridor of the central prison. Dzemo was taken out of his solitary cell. The two ladies were taken out from the floors. Sejo was taken from another part of the prison, and I was the only one to sign the piece of paper in the Cyrillic script, which -- I did it in spite, and the military policeman was not very happy. Still he had to release me. He didn't have a choice. I don't know what was contained on that piece of paper. I only knew that it meant freedom for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see your own name on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So you signed the document not knowing what it was about?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: At the time I must have known. I don't know now. I knew at the time that I was signing a document that was setting me free, that allowed me to go home. The policeman who brought me from the school to the central prison told me, "You're free now, but watch your mouth when you go back to work at the radio or wherever you work." I can't remember the contents of the document at the moment, but we were told we could go, we were free. We only had to sign that piece of paper, but I can't remember now what I was signing at the time. It was not a clean piece of paper, that I'm sure of. Something was written on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see any other document where -- provided for your released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the document, but a little later, maybe even a year later. I received it by fax. I don't know who from, from the western part of Mostar, and the message was, "You know what to do with this."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was that document about? I mean the document that you received later.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It was written in this document, "For the attention of Stanko Bozic, the head of the collection and investigation prison. The following prisoners should be released, Dzemo Andic [phoen], Alaliza [phoen], Bojana Mujanovic, Serboslokic [phoen], signed by Berislav Pusic."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit P 05949. Witness, is this the document you received by fax?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document that was faxed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Where were you taken from the mechanical faculty?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: They asked me where I resided. One of the policemen asked me on the ground floor of the building. I told him where I lived, because apparently they didn't know. They took me in front of my building. When I arrived there it was afternoon. At the door of my apartment there was a piece of paper which read that the apartment had been let out to somebody whose name I can't remember at the moment, but he was a member of the military police. There was a number, and the piece of paper was stamped, and I don't know who it was signed for -- signed by. On the 9th of May my wife and my two little children stayed back in the apartment, just to remind you of that. When I arrived there on that afternoon, the lock had been changed and there was a piece of paper to the effect that somebody had been living in the apartment, that the apartment had been rented out to that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did the document bear any stamp?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: There was a stamp, but I can't remember what kind of stamp. I believe that the certificate was issued to a member of the military police whose name I can't remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So did you report on the following day to the office for exchange of prisoners and other people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I reported to the office for exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Whom did you see there? To whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I reported to Mr. Pusic. Mr. Slobodan Lovrenovic was there as well, and also Mr. Jure Radic. Dr. Lugonja was there, and I can't remember his first name. They were all, save for Lovrenovic, who introduced himself to us as the head of Mr. Mate Boban's office. They were all talking to us, to the five of us. All five of us were in the office on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any options? Did they propose you options, where to go from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I learned on at that day that we were released at the intervention of the World Association of Journalists and News Publishers and the Centre for Independence from Ljubljana [as interpreted] In -- by Ms. Bojana Humar. On that occasion Mr. Lovrenovic gave us an opportunity to talk to Bojana and the question was raised as to what would happen to us. They had a huge problem in the office for exchanges, and they feared if we stayed in Mostar we would be killed. I didn't know where my wife and children were at that time. But since Mr. Pusic was in telephone contact with the other side, I learnt that on that day he had spoken to somebody on the other side and that my wife and children were in Jablanica. I was the only one, it seems to me, who was in favour of crossing over to the other side and joining my family. Dr. Lugonja told me at that moment that I could go even to the moon but not to the other side. Mr. Pusic suggested that since he was in contact with Zuka or somebody else from Jablanica that he would try and bring my wife and children over from Jablanica, that we would be joined in Mostar and then we would be sent all of us together to a third country from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But did he meet his promise?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It was impossible to do that. My -- my wife stayed there for a long time, and it took me a long time before I saw my wife and children again. I had to leave Mostar, and my wife remained in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you have any document when you were released from Heliodrom which would allow you not to be arrested by the first military police who would come to -- bump into you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, I didn't have a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps we can make a break, and I will take only a few minutes after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's almost half past 5.00. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Poryvaev.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Lizde, how long did you stay in Mostar after you had been released from Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Perhaps some 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you feel already free in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Relatively. Well, it was all the same to me, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Not -- not fully. Well, it was strange. No, I didn't feel completely free. There was still a lot of fighting in town going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were you supervised by anyone?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Not officially. However, I'm quite sure that I wasn't left to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you get any document which allowed you to cross the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive a document like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit P 0643. P 06433. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you find the document? Did you find --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is this a document you were given to just cross the Croatian border?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And the date of the document is the 4th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And for the records, by whom the document was signed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Mr. Berislav Pusic, head of the office for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Lizde, where were you supposed to go on from Croatia? What country did you -- make arrangements for you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Unfortunately I didn't make the arrangements, but in Zagreb I received a BH passport and a ticket to Istanbul; however, in Ljubljana, from the airport I managed to get to the embassy and I stayed in Ljubljana. I was supposed to go on to Turkey; however, I didn't, luckily.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When did you come back to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: On the 21st of February, 1994. I returned from Ancona and flew into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When did you see your family first?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I saw my family two or three days after that. That might have been the 25th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you get back your apartment in Mostar by now?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I did manage to have my apartment returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When did you get it back?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Two or three years ago. Just before the legal deadline.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And a couple more questions. Witness, were you interrogated at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. They did interrogate me at Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you make any statement, a written statement -- statement, in Heliodrom which was signed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The only statement that I signed throughout that time, throughout the time of the interrogation, that was the only one that I signed. So they interrogated me on one day, and the next day Mr. Vidovic came and gave me the document to sign, and that's the only statement that I actually signed during my stay in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So, Witness, is it correct that you were just interrogated at the mechanical faculty, at the MUP station, at Ljubuski, then Heliodrom, Dretelj? Did you see any accusation which was just put forward against you, official accusation, written accusation?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I was interrogated at all those places that you just mentioned, but up until now I have never received any kind of written accusation from anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have accomplished my examination-in-chief, but I have one issue to raise, and I think that we should go into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in open session. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you wanted to start, I presume?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. Lizde, I met you in December 1993, not personally, but I got to know you through your writings, in fact, the stories you wrote, whether you sent them from Sarajevo. I read it in the Oslobodjenje paper, "How I became a war criminal," that was one of the titles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And that was published in December 1993, was it, in -- as a series of six articles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We might go back to that series later on, but I'd like now to clarify certain matters to save time for all of us, the Trial Chamber and everybody else. As far as I've been able to understand you, you have known Mr. Pusic since before the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. His work took him quite near to where my offices were. So I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Right. You knew him. Now, on the basis of your testimony, I understand it that you met Mr. Pusic on the 7th of May, 1993, and that that was when you were released from Heliodrom in October 1993, and another meeting in Jablanica, but you don't know whether you actually talked to Mr. Pusic at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we could clarify certain matters straight away, not to waste time. On the 7th of May -- the 9th of May, 1993, you were a member of the BH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you mentioned a moment ago as having been given to the investigators, you gave two statements, actually. I think that's right. When you spoke about how you saw Mr. Pusic in chronological order, one -- in one portion, page 5 of the B/C/S version -- perhaps we could hand round the documents first for you all to be able to follow better. It is the statement of the 16th of January, 2004, and you say there when you met Mr. Pusic and how. And on -- on page 3 of the English text, it is in paragraph 14, you say: "I never saw Pusic when I was in Heliodrom, Dretelj, or Ljubuski." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now go back to the 7th of May, 1993. You've said that on that day you were arrested and that that was about noon, as far as I was able to gather, in front of your house.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: From my -- between my home and my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were taken away to the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And they detained you there, and you said five hours.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Until 5.00 or 6.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During that time nobody interrogated you? You didn't give any statements?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody mistreated you in any way?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, they did mistreat me when they took me to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I meant when you were at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, not then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I talked to Mr. Pusic, and he says he doesn't remember the meeting with you on the 7th of May, but let's start from that point. You said that you saw Mr. Pusic, who asked you what you were doing there. He said, "What are you doing here?" Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the way you intoned it I take it that Mr. Pusic was surprised to see you there.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what he said, and that's how I felt, he was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Was he alone? Did he have any escort, any security detail?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform. There might have been one or two soldiers with him, but he came up to me in that cellar. He came up to me alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the question he asked you, you said that he was surprised to see you, so I assume that he couldn't have known that you would be taken there or brought -- or that you had been brought to the mechanical engineering faculty.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't think anybody knew. They came across me in the street just by chance, but they needed to fill up a certain quota of men, and I happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time, or an unfortunate place at an unfortunate time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So when they released you at 6.00, was this a classical exchange or did they just say, "Mr. Lizde, you're free. You can go home"?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Nobody told me that. Nobody said "Mr. Lizde." They took us out of the cellar on two occasions. We lined up in front of the faculty building, and from the entrance door of the faculty to the gate of the Dzemo Bijedic university as it was called at the time from the gate to the entrance is about 300 metres, and there were quite a lot of us there. We were standing one next to another in line as you would in a classroom of pupils. They took us back because they didn't have enough of the other people released on the other side. At least that's what they told us. And nobody said, "Come on, Lizde," or, "Come on, so-and-so." The police just escorted us to the exit gate with their rifles and out on the street in front of the gate said we were free. They returned, and we went our separate ways. I, for example, went to the radio station because my colleagues waited for me there at the radio station, and my wife waited for me there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's go back to the series of articles that you wrote and the title was, "How I became a war criminal." You began with the 9th of May, 1993, and I didn't come across any chronology of events where you start with the 7th of May. Is that because the event wasn't that important because other reasons? I have to ask you that question.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. It's just journalistic approach and the amount of space I was given. I've also written a book. I'm sorry that you haven't read my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, you haven't. Had you read my book, you wouldn't be asking me that. But I began with the 9th of May because it's an interesting date. The 9th of May is the day when there was the battle or, rather it's the international World Day of the Fight Against Fascism, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to when you arrived in Jablanica. You arrived from Ancona to Sarajevo and Sarajevo, Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I came to fetch my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Was that in January?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No it was in February.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and make pauses between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, witness, speak less fast because it's hard for the interpreters to follow and also the interpreters are asking for breaks between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: We have a statement here, which you gave on the 7th of March, 1994, to the military police of the 4th Corps. That was right after your release, when I assume your memory was fresher than it is now. And you also start off with the 9th of May, 1993. You make no mention of the 7th of May, 1993, at all.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this wasn't interesting to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When I look at the introductory part, you say: "After he arrived," which means you arrived, "at this department, the military police battalion, because of his detention on the 7th of March, 1994," and then you continue to give, as you say, the following statement. I'm not challenging the fact that you were taken away on the 7th of May; I'm just telling you what the statement says. But what I kind noteworthy is that here, too, your starting date is the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: That may well be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's perfectly all right for you to go back to your statement and have a look, if you like. It's right there in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: As many others, if I may be allowed to, they probably also believed that that a six-hour detention is not much of a detention at all. They didn't see fit to record that. I did write down all the circumstances and in great detail myself. It helped me to remain sane. However, everything that I had to go through after those several hours at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering is hardly worth mentioning when compared to all the suffering that I underwent later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to the 19th of October, 1993. We heard about what you went through, Dretelj, Ljubuski, Heliodrom, and so on and so forth. On the 19th of October, 1993, you received a certificate, or at least that's what you said, at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, nobody gave me anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You signed it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I signed this in the central prison building. This document. I'm not sure what it said exactly, what it was about, but I signed and that meant I was free.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is not the same document that was faxed to you later on from West Mostar with the list of people to be freed; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, probably not. My signature is not there, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that you were released after pressure from the international journalists' association and from Ljubljana's journalist association.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It was pressure from IFG [as interpreted]. It's International Association of Journalists and Publishers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following document: This is 6D 00349. This is a statement from Habena. You know what that is; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's the Bosnian news agency. I suppose you've seen this, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's not a long document. I think you can just skim through it. This is a statement made by Vladislav Pogarcic, head of the human rights and humanitarian issues department with the office of the president of Herceg-Bosna. Does this reflect what you spoke about? Is this a result of what the -- this international association of journalist started?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't see that here. There's no reference to IFJ or the Ljubljana Association for Media Independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: But can this be a result of what they first started?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know. I find that very difficult to comment because I see nothing here to suggest that journalists requested our release. I see this as an act of goodwill.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If you don't know, that means we can't speak to it.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Especially since the investigation eventually showed something else, which is stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's just go back to this. On the 19th you're on your way. You signed the paper, and together with everybody else, with Bojana Mujanovic and Selma Dizdar and Sejo Beslagic and Mr. Andic, you arrive in Mr. Pusic's office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: This office is in the centre of town; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, it's known as the old Velez football stadium. It was actually in a flat in one of the buildings that were built just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The distance from Heliodrom would be several kilometres; right? As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Five or six, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Kilometres; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you spoke to Mr. Lugonja, to Mr. Radic, to Mr. Obrenovic. Mr. Lugonja told you what he told you, and Mr. Pusic tried there a way to make contact with your family so that you might be reunited with your family, but you said it wasn't realistic or feasible at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Eventually the Prosecutor showed you this document which is a request from Mr. Pusic's office to allow you to travel to Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I have a few questions. I just want to start with your background a little bit to make sure I understand it correctly. Now, back in -- in June 1993, you were -- you were questioned, were you not? You gave a statement to the Croatian Community of --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And it was in that statement that you indicated that part of your job with the information and propaganda service was to apply journalistic and literary finishing touches to the material which came from the information and propaganda unit. Do you recall making that -- saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Approximately, yeah. Roughly speaking. Something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I just --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: The wording itself I did find a bit strange sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So when you're talking about literary and journalistic finishing touches, is that correcting the grammar or is that sort of taking some poetic licence, as it were, with the content, because, as you know, journalists have to sometimes have to make a story -- have to spice it up in order to make it appealing to the audience?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, both. It was the syntax but I didn't really touch up the substance as it related to anyone else. I produced my own substance. Substance. But, you know, we had to chisel up a sentence or two so because that's what journalists do, don't they.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, and sometimes they embellish a little bit too. So would you take the licence of embellishing if it meant making the story a little more persuasive, a little more compelling for the audience? After all, part of your job is to grab the attention of the audience and keep them and hopefully even get more people to listen to you or to read your press, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, as far as that period was concerned, I don't think you could say that we had to really fight for people to listen to us. We had listeners. We sure did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could answer my question there.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Most of them were --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, would you embellish if necessary? I guess that's the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. That's not your -- that's not how you operate, I take it.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by embellishing. I think that's a clumsy term, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Embellishing would be, say, making something up.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No, certainly not. I never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you gave also a statement in 2002 to the Office of the Prosecutor, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it, sticking to your journalistic ethics, when you were recounting the events as you would write about or cover events in your profession, you did not embellish at all either when you were giving your statement. In other words, you just told the facts as you understood it or remembered them to be?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part. Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You told us you went to Prozor to cover that event. At some point you went to Prozor; right? And you said you came back. And that would have been in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you came back and you wanted to maybe -- to broadcast, to report about it; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that point in time, were your offices in the Vranica building? Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, from the very outset that's where the offices were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure because I -- you know, the dates confuse me a little bit. And that was the same building that also had the headquarters of the army of BiH; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so there would have been security there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And security with -- with arms?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, like any security you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at that time you were working essentially what -- don't take this the wrong way, but am I to understand that this radio station was sort of connected to, associated with part of the army of BiH?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No. There was no association.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So in other words, this was strictly civilian, had nothing to do with the military, nothing to do with -- it just -- it just happened to -- by serendipity, to find space right by the headquarters of ABiH. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say it was a coincidence. It was for security reasons that the officers were there, and I was the link between the army and the radio station, and I was one of the editors, as you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in that statement -- and thank you for that answer, and I'm going to press you just a little bit, because I found something rather curious in your statement of 2002, which I didn't hear today. You testified under oath. And I certainly didn't see it repeated, albeit you might not have been asked about it in your statement of 2004, but in your statement of 2002 you say that when the message was delivered to you that you could not broadcast, the gentleman that had brought the message to you put a gun to your head. That's what you said. Now, first question is do you recall making the statement? And that's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I made the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: -- and that's indeed how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you would agree with me under oath today that you didn't say anything about somebody delivering a statement and pointing a gun to your head. I mean, it's not in the transcript and we can get it. So you either said it or you didn't say. Now, do you recall saying that today? Yes, no, maybe, I don't recall. Which of the four? That's all I need.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I didn't mention that today. I did expect a question from the OTP, and they said, "Was it on that piece of paper or not?" I said he walked in with that gun but I never said that he placed this gun against my head, so I'm saying what I said back in 2002 was correct. Mr. Zeljko Dzida walked in with a gun --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: -- and that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. He walked in with the gun and was the gun to his side inside a holster?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I kept a diary. We were live on the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me read to you what you've said here, and we can give you the version in your language. And incidentally I should tell you that on every page you have initialed it, at least the English part, but in any event, let me read to you what it says here. It says that, "A little after 1600 hours HVO police chief Dzidic, Zeljko, aka Dzida, had come to the radio station. Present were also Kuko Senad." I hope I'm pronouncing it correctly, but I'm sure you get the drift. And -- and Manjgo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you be so kind as to indicate the page from which you're quoting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise. Page 4, it's page 4. I certainly apologise. And this would be -- and I don't have the number of the exhibit -- the exhibit number because it's not in, but this is something I wasn't -- I expected the gentleman to say such an important event on direct but obviously he didn't but we'll cure that little technicality. And this would be, Your Honours, on page 4 and it's one, two, three four, the fifth paragraph, the fifth paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so if I can pick up where I left off. "... aka Kuko Senad and Manjgo Asim who was in charge of the tones. Dzida came in with a piece of paper in his hands, took a pistol, pointed it at my head and told me to read what was written on the paper. I read." And then you go on. Then in the following paragraph you say as you have said on occasion, you have commented when you thought something was noteworthy, you say: "The other interesting thing," that's part of your patois, it would appear, you know, "The other interesting thing was that Dzida had to pass through the security in the headquarters of the ABiH to come to the basement where the radio was. When he came in the room I was in, pointing the gun at my forehead. I thought that he had just killed -- I thought that he had just killed everybody." And then you go on. Now, I take it you don't deny making that statement back then in 2002 to the Office of the Prosecutor; right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so when you were being asked questions by the Prosecutor, because he did ask you more than one question about the delivery of the message that you had to stop broadcasting, you didn't mention any of that under oath; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't think I understood you. Can you please repeat that for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Let me -- I'll -- when you were being asked to describe the event, the event that is of this individual coming to deliver the notice to you, you did not describe any of that -- anything that I've just read from your 2002 statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I gave a statement in 2002, didn't I. Do you expect me to say that a thousand times perhaps? I'm telling you again. I'm telling you again exactly what I said back in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When I -- did you say that under oath today on direct examination when questioned by the Prosecutor after he took you in his office and proofed you so you would be prepared to answer his questions here today? Did you say that today on direct examination when he was questioning you? That's a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I didn't mention that today, but I mentioned it back in 2002, and I'm telling you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir -- help me how out here now. Would you agree with me that this is something noteworthy? This is something significant? This is something you would just not pass over and omit to say, especially if you've come here to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? And what I'm suggesting is -- and what I'm suggesting is, so I can drive my point home is: Sir, you are a man that embellishes, and it may be a professional habit, but you are someone who embellishes on the facts, and at least in 2002 you were embellishing on the facts, and that's the point I'm trying to drive home right now. And what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I never added anything to the facts during my interview with this investigator, which was a brief one. That's the one you're referring to. I don't see fit then or today when answering questions by the OTP as to what Dzida brought me. He brought me a slip of paper. I just focused on the fact that there was a note on that slip of paper. He was adamant that I should say what I read on that slip of paper. I said he was armed. Of course he was. He went past the security at the Vranica building and he pulled out a gun and placed it against my temple. I said that back in 2002 and I'm still saying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're saying it now; you didn't say it on direct. But that's besides the point. We'll move on. I'm going to go through some documents here and again we're going to move rather quickly. Oh, I'm told I have to deliver the documents. If I can get the assistance of the usher. We're moving quicker than we anticipated, and it may be that we will all conclude by tomorrow. There's a good possibility. Okay. Sir, before you go through the documents, we're going to go one by one, okay, to save time. The first document is 1D 01414. There's no need for a lot of commentary. I just want to point a few things out to the Trial Chamber. Do you recognise this document, sir? It's a yes or a no. Have you ever seen it? You can look at the page --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's a no.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have the -- if you look at the third or fourth page, you'll see that it's in -- it's in your language. Have you seen that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. I know that this was published, but I've never seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: It's a magazine for culture, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And we see here it was published in Mostar in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And just for the Court's benefit, we see that there's -- you can purchase it in either Croatian dinars, Deutschmarks, or BiH dinars. So we have a choice as to what sort of currency. And that's all we need at this point in time right now with this particular document. You know, I'm sure the Court can -- will find the one area where -- I believe it's on third page in English where they wish to thank their friends for the publishing of that. But that's all I wanted to point out for that document. Now, if we go to the next document. It's 1D 01415. And again very quickly. You have the original version. Okay. "Mostar morning." Have you ever heard of that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And here it talks about May -- we have a date of May 22nd, 1992. That would have been published back then, would it not? I mean June. June 11, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the 1st of November [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So June 11, 1992, we do in fact have -- we do in fact have publications in Mostar by the Muslim community; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: This is a publication by the 1st Mostar Brigade. I wouldn't say that it belongs to the Muslim community. The 1st Mostar Brigade was made up of Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And I think that's -- now just for the benefit of the record, if we could go to page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: There's just a greeting from the HVO of Mostar municipality headquarters. I just wish to point this out to the Judges at this point in time. And again, keep -- and then again keeping in mind the date. And then if we go on to page 4, also by the Croatian Community, you will see a greetings and wishes for the holiday of Kurban Bajram. So that's all we need for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, sir, don't worry. You're being used as sort of a conduit to get documents in that may be relevant at some other point. It may also have to deal with some of your testimony as well. If we could go to the next document, 1D 01416. 1416. Okay. And here in this document is dated August 24, 1992. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And here is a -- and this is a list of employees? You know, for the radio station Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't an employee myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But on that list do you see any Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you count and tell us more or less how many of them do you see?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I don't know which of these people really feel Muslims. That's the question, and I'm not one to count them, am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean when you say "Muslim"? What's in a name? A name means nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me -- well, they were at the time a constituent peoples; right? That's what they were called before they changed to Bosniak; right? I don't mean any disrespect in that manner. Right? Okay but --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Okay. I simply don't know which of these were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me help you out.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Zlata cuts both ways. Could be Muslim, could be something else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay, what about number 5. Omer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object. It seems to me Mr. Karnavas is flogging a dead horse. The response has been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't think this horse is being flogged nor is it dead, but if we could just go down the list, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Number 5, Omer. Is that a Muslim name? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's a Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... number 6?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: As to whether this particular Omer is a Muslim or not, I really can't be expected to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... number 6. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Anes. Anes is a very lovely Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: But I don't know whether this particular Anes is a Muslim or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Number 7. Mirela.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. That could cut both ways, you say. Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LIZDE
utterances.text: Yes.
